label: Duality
notes: Open by naming duality as the chapter's organizing move. The lecture starts with the algebraic dual of a chain group, then turns that bookkeeping into geometric complementarity. Keep the provenance visible but brief: Chapter 05, printed pages 103-124, physical PDF pages 116-137, with exercises starting on printed page 123.

label: Why Duality
notes: Use this as the motivation map. Duality is not one theorem but a repeating translation: cycles become tests, tests become complementary blocks, complementary blocks become intersections, and intersections become fast classification rules. Tell students that every later slide should answer what is being translated and what information is preserved.

label: Cochains
notes: Emphasize that a cochain is an observer of chains. Over Z2 it reports parity, so the evaluation can be read as whether the selected simplices meet the tested chain an odd number of times. This simple parity viewpoint is the seed of the later intersection pairing.

label: Coboundary
notes: Make the coboundary feel operational. A boundary lowers dimension by taking faces, while the coboundary raises dimension by asking which cofaces see the chosen simplex. The displayed identity is the whole mechanism: evaluating before a boundary equals evaluating after a coboundary.

label: Cohomology Groups
notes: Treat this slide as the mirror of the homology definition. Cocycles are cochains whose coboundary vanishes, coboundaries are those already produced from one dimension below, and the quotient records the tests that detect genuine topology rather than a local potential.

label: Annulus Example
notes: Read the annulus through two picket fences. A fence that closes around a region is a coboundary, while a radial fence from one boundary component to the other cannot be globally filled by a vertex potential. That single obstruction gives the H1 generator.

label: Matrix View
notes: Connect the visual story to computation. Once bases are chosen, the coboundary matrix is exactly the transpose of the next boundary matrix over Z2. Therefore the same normal form data that computes homology ranks also computes cohomology ranks, only read from the dual side.

label: Combinatorial Manifolds
notes: Before stating Poincare duality, slow down on the manifold hypothesis. The link condition guarantees that local neighborhoods behave like balls and spheres, so dual blocks have the expected complementary dimensions. Without that local control, the dual block proof can lose its geometric meaning.

label: Dual Blocks
notes: Use the diagram as a construction recipe. Barycentric subdivision supplies a vertex for every simplex, and the dual block of sigma consists of subdivided simplices where sigma is the smallest face in the chain. Face relations reverse, which is why the boundary of a dual block is built from cofaces.

label: Poincare Duality, First Form
notes: Present the proof as a commuting square rather than as a mysterious isomorphism. Map each dual block to the cochain that selects the corresponding primal simplex. Both routes around the square select exactly the cofaces of sigma, so the chain-level correspondence descends to homology and cohomology.

label: Intersection Numbers
notes: Intersection is the geometric reading of the same duality map. In complementary dimensions, count intersection points modulo two. The important point is well-definedness: if either cycle is changed by a boundary, intersections are created or removed in pairs, so the parity is unchanged.

label: Perfect Pairing
notes: A perfect pairing means no nonzero class is invisible to all complementary classes. Algebraically, the pairing identifies one homology group with the dual vector space of the other. This is the second form of Poincare duality and the bridge from geometry back to linear algebra.

label: Torus Versus Klein Bottle
notes: This comparison prevents a common misconception. The torus and Klein bottle have the same Z2 Betti numbers, but their intersection forms differ. On the Klein bottle, the one-sided curve has self-intersection one after push-off, so the pairing records more than just ranks.

label: Lefschetz Duality
notes: Explain Lefschetz duality as the boundary-corrected version of Poincare duality. Absolute classes pair with relative classes because complementary chains may now have endpoints or boundaries on the boundary of the manifold. The half-torus picture makes the relative generator visible.

label: Alexander Duality
notes: Alexander duality shifts attention from a manifold to its complement in a sphere. A p-dimensional reduced homology class in N corresponds to a complementary class in the dual block complex X of dimension d minus p minus one. The toy circle in S2 shows the dimension shift.

label: Algorithmic Payoff
notes: Now turn the theorems into an algorithm. Adding one simplex either creates a new class in its own dimension or kills a class one dimension lower. Once a simplex has been classified as positive or negative, the Betti update is constant time.

label: S3 Classification
notes: For complexes in S3, the low and high dimensional classifications become cheap. Vertices and edges are handled with ordinary union-find on components, while tetrahedra and triangles are handled from the complementary dual perspective. Alexander duality justifies reading triangles through reverse dual edges.

label: Recap / Instructor Prompt
notes: Close by asking students to trace one object through the whole chain of translations. A simplex becomes a cochain, a cochain becomes a dual block, a dual block participates in an intersection number, and the same complementarity powers the incremental Betti algorithm. The prompt should surface any weak link in that story.
